item.title: When Should You Text After a First Date?
item.description:
Mating

When Should You Text After a First Date?

Women may be especially sensitive to the timing of post-date texts.

Posted September 26, 2026

Key points
  • When people should text after their first date has long been a point of uncertainty.
  • A survey showed that people think a moderate time is best, and experimental evidence offers support.
  • Research showed that texting the next day elicits the strongest relationship intentions, particular for women.
  • Women are more sensitive to the timing of texts, but both men and women think early texting signals neediness.

Great first date. Now you're home. What do you do? Do you send a text? Tonight? Tomorrow? In three days?

Uncertainty reigns. Text too soon, you could give the impression that you're desperate. Wait too long, you might inadvertently signal that you're not interested, that you're "too cool" to be worth the effort. You waffle between your options, with no clear best move. Is there any way to win?

When does sending a text lead the other person to have the greatest intentions of pursing the relationship?

People often talk about rules, like the three day rule or the don't-text-first rule, but none of these is empirically based. In other words, the uncertainty people feel in this context reflects a reality: no one has submitted this question to scientific scrutiny. Until now.

3 Possible Outcomes for the Timing of a Post-Date Text

New research (finally!) used experimental methods to investigate the age-old question of when a person should extend the first follow-up after a first date (Teichmann et al., 2026). Thinking through the puzzle, the researchers offered three possibilities, which I'm calling:

  1. To Wait is to Win. Maybe playing hard-to-get is the best bet. It builds intrigue, potentially making you seem more desirable. In this case, texting late (after what might be typical) could inspire more relationship intention and help build romantic chemistry.
  2. Sooner is Better. Another possibility is that early texts spark romantic interest. Consider the benefits of showing confidence. People might be attracted to a person who messages sooner than typical. No games, just interest.
  3. The Expected Moment. Maybe what works best is texting after a moderate amount of time, i.e., the time that most people think is normative. This model reflects an upside-down "U," with relationship outcomes on the Y-axis (higher is better) and time on the X-axis.

Which of these competing possibilities seems most on point?

Survey Data Reveal When People Think Is the Best Time

Researchers first conducted an online survey asking 50 men and 50 women about their perceptions of the "ideal time" for a post-date text (Teichmann et al., 2026).

  • The best time. Participants indicated that about 6 hours after the date, on average, would be a good time to reach out. Note the standard deviation was over 10 hours, suggesting a fair amount of disagreement. The researchers operationalized this potentially ideal time as "the next morning."
  • Too soon. Participants showed moderate agreement that right after the date (i.e., 20 minutes later, give or take three hours) would be too soon.
  • Too late. When asked when would be "too late," people indicated 40 hours, on average. However, once again, the data showed impressive variability, with a standard deviation of 34 hours.

Manipulating Timing and Measuring Interest

The researchers then switched from a survey to a laboratory experiment (Teichmann et al., 2026). Their 543 participants read a story about a pretend date at an Italian restaurant, and were randomly assigned to read that the person followed up by texting right after saying goodbye ("soon"), the next morning ("moderate time") or after two days ("waiting"). Participants then reported their level of intention to pursue the relationship, as well as chemistry and motivation to reconnect.

In other words, by manipulating the timing of the text, researchers could reveal how the timing actually affects romantic intention, chemistry, and motivation.

Best Strategy? Go with Goldilocks

Researchers found general support for an upside-down "U" curve, where time is on the X-axis and relationship intention on the Y-axis (Teichmann et al., 2026). In other words, go for a moderate amount of time: not too soon, not too late, just right.

For felt chemistry and motivation to reconnect, the pattern was more linear, suggesting (in general) that early or after a moderate amount of time is better than late. The right away and next day texts did not differ in their elicitation of felt chemistry or motivation to move the relationship forward.

Women React More to Text Timing

These general trends aside, another interesting finding emerged. Women may be more sensitive to the timing of a post-date text than men (Teichmann et al., 2026).

Women showed a steeper rise and then drop in their relationship intentions over time, as a function of when they were told they received their first post-date text. The best time? The next day.

Interestingly, if not the standard "moderate" amount of time, women on the whole preferred an early text to a late text. An early text elicited more favorable outcomes than a late text, though neither was as favorable as the next day. But, be wary of being seen as "too needy," a quality that women did suggest early texts convey.

Men did not differentiate between a "too early" text and the typical text of the next day in terms of their romantic interest, but they did see early texters as needy. Only the late text appeared to elicit less favorable responses than the earlier texts.

Men and Women Infer Liking from Text Timing

Both men and women inferred how much the person liked them from when they received their post-date text (Teichmann et al., 2026). Receiving a text right away meant more liking than the next day, and two days later suggested the least amount of liking. Receiving a text two days later amounted to a significant drop in perceived liking for both men and women, but especially women on the receiving end of those texts.

This suggests that men who want to show they like a women shouldn't wait three days to reach out. That timing changes the message they might wish to send.

The Take-Away

This research offers actionable suggestions about how to best approach the first post-date text. Forget about playing hard-to-get: a better approach, one that can signal reliability and liking, is to text after a moderate amount of time, i.e., the next day. If not the next day, right after the date is an appropriate strategy, though you risk suggesting neediness (though also high liking).

Chances of maintaining the other person's interest in starting the relationship seems to be markedly lower if you wait to text until two days later.

The study focused on heterosexual individuals, so its generalizability is limited: additional research could look at same-gendered relationships. In different-gendered relationships, an additional question might be who should text first: men or women?

Finally, and most pressingly, the researchers did not tackle is what the text might say. That is an entirely other uncertainty. The next research study, perhaps?
